claim: C. elegans has a single Shank gene, shn-1
source: C. elegans has a single Shank gene, shn-1.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: The SHN-1 protein lacks an SH3 domain but has all other domains found in mammalian Shank proteins
source: The SHN-1 protein lacks an SH3 domain but has all other domains found in mammalian Shank proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing protein domain comparison

claim: SHN-1's PDZ domain binds the EGL-19 carboxy-terminal motif (-VTTLCOOH) by yeast two-hybrid assay
source: We confirmed that SHN-1's PDZ domain binds the EGL-19 carboxy-terminal motif (-VTTLCOOH) by both yeast two-hybrid and GST-pull down assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Experimental data from yeast two-hybrid and GST-pull down assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: SHN-1's PDZ domain binds the EGL-19 carboxy-terminal motif (-VTTLCOOH) by GST-pull down assay
source: We confirmed that SHN-1's PDZ domain binds the EGL-19 carboxy-terminal motif (-VTTLCOOH) by both yeast two-hybrid and GST-pull down assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Experimental data from GST-pull down assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: SHN-1 binds to EGL-19/Cav1 like their mammalian counterparts
source: Thus, like their mammalian counterparts, SHN-1 binds to EGL-19/ Cav1 (Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: shn-1 mutants had significantly decreased Ca+2 current-density
source: In shn-1(tm488) null mutants, calcium current density was significantly decreased (Figure 1B,C,E).

claim: The voltage-dependence of calcium current activation was not altered in shn-1(tm488) null mutants
source: Neither the voltage-dependence of calcium current activation (Figure 1D) nor the deactivation kinetics (Figure 1F) were altered in shn-1(tm488) null mutants.

claim: The deactivation kinetics were not altered in shn-1(tm488) null mutants
source: Neither the voltage-dependence of calcium current activation (Figure 1D) nor the deactivation kinetics (Figure 1F) were altered in shn-1(tm488) null mutants.

claim: The shn-1 calcium current defect was rescued by a transgene restoring SHN-1 expression in body muscles
source: The shn-1 calcium current defect was rescued by a transgene restoring SHN-1 expression in body muscles (Figure 1E), confirming that SHN-1 has a cell autonomous effect on EGL-19/Cav1 currrent.
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1E

claim: SHN-1 has a cell autonomous effect on EGL-19/Cav1 current
source: The shn-1 calcium current defect was rescued by a transgene restoring SHN-1 expression in body muscles (Figure 1E), confirming that SHN-1 has a cell autonomous effect on EGL-19/Cav1 currrent.

claim: The voltage-dependence of fast and slow potassium currents were not significantly altered in shn-1 mutants
source: Neither the voltage-dependence nor the current density of fast and slow potassium currents were significantly altered in shn-1 mutants.

claim: The current density of fast and slow potassium currents were not significantly altered in shn-1 mutants
source: Neither the voltage-dependence nor the current density of fast and slow potassium currents were significantly altered in shn-1 mutants.

claim: SHN-1 specifically regulates the expression or function of EGL-19/Cav1 channels
source: Collectively, these results suggest that SHN-1 specifically regulates the expression or function of EGL-19/Cav1 channels.
evidence: Inferred from selective effect on calcium but not potassium currents

claim: Both egl-19 deletion mutants (nu495 and nu496) exhibited decreased calcium current density similar to the defect observed in shn-1 null mutants
source: Both deletion mutants exhibited decreased calcium current density (similar to the defect observed in shn-1 null mutants) (Figure 2B–C).

claim: The egl-19(nu496) mutation had no effect on the voltage-dependence of calcium current activation
source: The egl-19(nu496) mutation had no effect on the voltage-dependence of calcium current activation nor on deactivation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: The egl-19(nu496) mutation had no effect on deactivation kinetics
source: The egl-19(nu496) mutation had no effect on the voltage-dependence of calcium current activation nor on deactivation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: The egl-19(nu496) and shn-1 null mutations did not have additive effects on calcium current density in double mutants
source: The egl-19(nu496) and shn-1 null mutations did not have additive effects on calcium current density in double mutants, as would be predicted if SHN-1's effects on calcium current require direct binding to EGL-19's carboxy-terminus (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: SHN-1's effects on calcium current require direct binding to EGL-19's carboxy-terminus
source: The egl-19(nu496) and shn-1 null mutations did not have additive effects on calcium current density in double mutants, as would be predicted if SHN-1's effects on calcium current require direct binding to EGL-19's carboxy-terminus (Figure 2D and E).

claim: The shn-1(ok1241) mutants exhibited a decrease in calcium current density similar to those observed in shn-1 null and the egl-19 carboxy-terminal deletion mutants
source: The shn-1(ok1241) mutants exhibited a decrease in calcium current density similar to those observed in shn-1 null and the egl-19 carboxy-terminal deletion mutants and had no effect on voltage-dependence of current activation nor on deactivation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F

claim: The shn-1(ok1241) mutation had no effect on voltage-dependence of current activation
source: The shn-1(ok1241) mutants exhibited a decrease in calcium current density similar to those observed in shn-1 null and the egl-19 carboxy-terminal deletion mutants and had no effect on voltage-dependence of current activation nor on deactivation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F

claim: The shn-1(ok1241) mutation had no effect on deactivation kinetics
source: The shn-1(ok1241) mutants exhibited a decrease in calcium current density similar to those observed in shn-1 null and the egl-19 carboxy-terminal deletion mutants and had no effect on voltage-dependence of current activation nor on deactivation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F

claim: SHN-1 binding to EGL-19's carboxy-terminus promotes the expression or function of L-type calcium channels
source: Collectively, these results suggest that SHN-1 binding to EGL-19's carboxy-terminus promotes the expression or function of L-type calcium channels.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and biochemical data

claim: The total voltage activated gating charge in body muscles was significantly reduced in shn-1 null mutants
source: The total voltage activated gating charge in body muscles was significantly reduced in shn-1 null mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: Gating current measurements shown in Figure 3B

claim: The decreased calcium current exhibited in shn-1 mutants arises from decreased trafficking of EGL-19/Cav1 channels to the cell surface
source: Thus, analysis of gating currents suggests that the decreased calcium current exhibited in shn-1 mutants arises from decreased trafficking of EGL-19/Cav1 channels to the cell surface.

claim: In shn-1 null mutants, the intensity and size of green Terrier puncta were significantly decreased
source: In shn-1 null mutants, the intensity and size of green Terrier puncta were significantly decreased (Figure 3D–G), indicating decreased surface Terrier protein in the nerve ring.
evidence: Fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3D–G

claim: shn-1 null mutants show decreased surface Terrier protein in the nerve ring
source: In shn-1 null mutants, the intensity and size of green Terrier puncta were significantly decreased (Figure 3D–G), indicating decreased surface Terrier protein in the nerve ring.

claim: Decreased calcium current density (20%) in shn-1 mutants was mirrored by similar decreases in gating charge (26%) and total surface Terrier fluorescence (36%)
source: Thus, decreased calcium current density (20%) in shn-1 mutants was mirrored by similar decreases in gating charge (26%) and total surface Terrier fluorescence (36%).

claim: The decreased calcium current in shn-1 null mutants arises from decreased delivery of EGL-19/Cav1 channels to the cell surface
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the decreased calcium current in shn-1 null mutants arises from decreased delivery of EGL-19/Cav1 channels to the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from gating current and Terrier fluorescence data

claim: Cav1 channels account for a small fraction of bulk calcium entry in neurons
source: Although Cav1 channels account for a small fraction of bulk calcium entry in neurons, Cav1 channels account for the majority of activity-induced gene expression (Ma et al., 2012).

claim: Cav1 channels account for the majority of activity-induced gene expression
source: Although Cav1 channels account for a small fraction of bulk calcium entry in neurons, Cav1 channels account for the majority of activity-induced gene expression (Ma et al., 2012).

claim: The privileged ability of Cav1 channels to activate gene expression is thought to be mediated by direct physical coupling of Cav1 channels to the calcium sensors responsible for activating CREB
source: This privileged ability of Cav1 channels to activate gene expression is thought to be mediated by direct physical coupling of Cav1 channels to the calcium sensors responsible for activating CREB (Deisseroth et al., 1996; Wheeler et al., 2008).

claim: 427 genes were significantly increased in expression following muscle depolarization with levamisole (>2 fold change, FDR p<0.05)
source: This analysis identified 427 genes whose expression was significantly increased following muscle depolarization (>2 fold change, FDR p<0.05) (Figure 4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Microarray data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 2

claim: 67% (287/427) of Lev-induced genes contain binding sites for the myogenic transcription factor HLH-1 (<5 kb from the transcriptional start site, TSS)
source: 67% (287/427) of Lev-induced genes contain binding sites for the myogenic transcription factor HLH-1 (<5 kb from the transcriptional start site, TSS) in chromatin-immunoprecipitation experiments (http://www.modencode.org), suggesting that these genes are expressed in body muscles.
evidence: Analysis of ChIP-seq data from modENCODE

claim: 81% (233/287) of HLH-1 binding genes contain predicted CREB binding sites (<5 kb from the TSS)
source: Of the HLH-1 binding genes, 81% (233/287) contain predicted CREB binding sites (<5 kb from the TSS).

claim: C. elegans body muscles have a large number of activity-induced genes, many of which are potential CREB transcriptional targets
source: These results suggest that C. elegans body muscles (like other excitable cells) have a large number of activity-induced genes, many of which are potential CREB transcriptional targets.
evidence: Inferred from microarray and promoter analysis

claim: gem-4/Copine gene was the top hit from the analysis of Lev-induced genes (induced ~30 fold)
source: For this purpose, we focused on the gem-4/Copine gene, which was the top hit from our analysis of Lev-induced genes (induced ~30 fold) (Figure 4).

claim: The gem-4 promoter contains multiple CRH-1/CREB binding sites
source: The gem-4 promoter contains multiple CRH-1/CREB binding sites, implying that it could be a direct CRH-1 transcriptional target.

claim: Lev treatment increased gem-4 mRNA levels 8-fold
source: Quantitative RT-PCR confirmed that Lev treatment increased gem-4 mRNA levels 8-fold (Figure 5A).

claim: Lev treatment increased gem-4 expression 8–12-fold
source: Using this reporter, we found that Lev treatment increased gem-4 expression 8–12-fold (Figure 5C–D) while myo-3 expression was unaltered (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Reporter assay data shown in Figure 5C–D

claim: myo-3 expression was unaltered by Lev treatment
source: Using this reporter, we found that Lev treatment increased gem-4 expression 8–12-fold (Figure 5C–D) while myo-3 expression was unaltered (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Lev-induction of the gem-4 reporter was eliminated by mutations inactivating a Lev receptor subunit (UNC-29)
source: Lev-induction of the gem-4 reporter was eliminated by mutations inactivating a Lev receptor subunit (UNC-29), indicating that gem-4 induction was not mediated by an off target effect of Lev (Figure 5C).
evidence: Genetic control experiment shown in Figure 5C

claim: gem-4 induction was not mediated by an off target effect of Lev
source: Lev-induction of the gem-4 reporter was eliminated by mutations inactivating a Lev receptor subunit (UNC-29), indicating that gem-4 induction was not mediated by an off target effect of Lev (Figure 5C).

claim: Lev-induction of gem-4 was blocked in mutants lacking CRH-1/CREB
source: Lev-induction of gem-4 was also blocked in mutants lacking CRH-1/CREB and this defect was rescued by a transgene expressing CRH-1 in body muscles (Figure 5D).

claim: The crh-1 mutant defect in gem-4 induction was rescued by a transgene expressing CRH-1 in body muscles
source: Lev-induction of gem-4 was also blocked in mutants lacking CRH-1/CREB and this defect was rescued by a transgene expressing CRH-1 in body muscles (Figure 5D).

claim: gem-4 is a CRH-1/CREB target expressed in body muscles
source: These results identify gem-4 as a CRH-1/CREB target expressed in body muscles.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and expression data

claim: The gem-4 reporter was significantly induced following 2, 5, 10, and 20 Hz photo-stimulation
source: The gem-4 reporter was significantly induced following 2, 5, 10, and 20 Hz photo-stimulation (Figure 5E).
evidence: Optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 5E

claim: gem-4 induction was not observed at 0.5 and 1 Hz photo-stimulation
source: Induction was not observed at lower frequencies (0.5 and 1 Hz) nor when animals were cultured without all trans-retinal (ATR) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 5E

claim: gem-4 induction was not observed when animals were cultured without all trans-retinal (ATR)
source: Induction was not observed at lower frequencies (0.5 and 1 Hz) nor when animals were cultured without all trans-retinal (ATR) (Figure 5E).

claim: Photo-induction of gem-4 expression was eliminated in unc-13 mutants
source: Photo-induction of gem-4 expression was eliminated in unc-13 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which have dramatically reduced synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Richmond et al., 1999).
evidence: Genetic experiment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: unc-13 mutations did not prevent Lev-induced gem-4 expression
source: By contrast, unc-13 mutations did not prevent Lev-induced gem-4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Genetic experiment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Similar levels of gem-4 induction were produced by 20 Hz photo-stimulation and Lev treatment
source: Similar levels of gem-4 induction were produced by 20 Hz photo-stimulation and Lev treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Comparison of data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: The gem-4 reporter was induced by both synaptic and Lev-evoked muscle depolarization
source: Thus, the gem-4 reporter was induced by both synaptic and Lev-evoked muscle depolarization.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic and pharmacological stimulation data

claim: Expression of a mouse gem-4 paralog (N-copine) in hippocampal neurons is induced by high frequency stimulation of acute brain slices
source: Expression of a mouse gem-4 paralog (N-copine) in hippocampal neurons is also induced by high frequency stimulation of acute brain slices (Nakayama et al., 1998); consequently, activity-induced copine expression is observed in both muscles and neurons and is conserved across phylogeny.

claim: Activity-induced copine expression is observed in both muscles and neurons and is conserved across phylogeny
source: Expression of a mouse gem-4 paralog (N-copine) in hippocampal neurons is also induced by high frequency stimulation of acute brain slices (Nakayama et al., 1998); consequently, activity-induced copine expression is observed in both muscles and neurons and is conserved across phylogeny.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of C. elegans and mouse data

claim: Lev-induced gem-4 expression was significantly decreased in shn-1(tm488) null mutants
source: Lev-induced gem-4 expression was significantly decreased in shn-1(tm488) null mutants (Figure 5F).
evidence: Reporter assay data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Expression of the cex-1 reporter in body muscles was dramatically induced following Lev treatment
source: Expression of the cex-1 reporter in body muscles was dramatically induced following Lev treatment (Figure 5J).
evidence: Reporter assay data shown in Figure 5J

claim: Lev-induced cex-1 expression in muscles was dramatically reduced in shn-1 null mutants
source: As seen with the gem-4 reporter, we found that Lev-induced cex-1 expression in muscles was dramatically reduced in shn-1 null mutants (Figure 5J).
evidence: Reporter assay data shown in Figure 5J

claim: SHN-1 promotes activity-induced gene expression in body muscles
source: Taken together, these results support the idea that SHN-1 promotes activity-induced gene expression in body muscles.
evidence: Inferred from gem-4 and cex-1 reporter data

claim: Deleting EGL-19's PDZ ligand [in egl-19(nu496) mutants] significantly increased gem-4 induction
source: Deleting EGL-19's PDZ ligand [in egl-19(nu496) mutants] significantly increased gem-4 induction while deleting SHN-1's PDZ domain [in shn-1(ok1241) mutants] had no effect on gem-4 induction (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: Reporter assay data shown in Figure 5G–H

claim: Deleting SHN-1's PDZ domain [in shn-1(ok1241) mutants] had no effect on gem-4 induction
source: Deleting EGL-19's PDZ ligand [in egl-19(nu496) mutants] significantly increased gem-4 induction while deleting SHN-1's PDZ domain [in shn-1(ok1241) mutants] had no effect on gem-4 induction (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: Reporter assay data shown in Figure 5G–H

claim: SHN-1 regulates EGL-19/Cav1 current and CRH-1/CREB activation by distinct mechanisms
source: These results indicate that SHN-1 regulates EGL-19/Cav1 current and CRH-1/CREB activation by distinct mechanisms, since the former requires PDZ binding to EGL-19 while the latter does not.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of PDZ domain mutations

claim: Muscle calcium current density was significantly increased in animals containing 1 and 4 copies of shn-1 compared to wild type controls
source: Compared to wild type controls, muscle calcium current density was significantly increased in animals containing 1 and 4 copies of shn-1 and was significantly decreased in animals containing 0 copies of shn-1 (Figure 6A–C).

claim: Muscle calcium current density was significantly decreased in animals containing 0 copies of shn-1 compared to wild type controls
source: Compared to wild type controls, muscle calcium current density was significantly increased in animals containing 1 and 4 copies of shn-1 and was significantly decreased in animals containing 0 copies of shn-1 (Figure 6A–C).

claim: The kinetics of calcium current deactivation were not significantly altered by changes in shn-1 dosage
source: The kinetics of calcium current deactivation were not significantly altered by changes in shn-1 dosage (Figure 6D).

claim: gem-4 induction was significantly diminished in animals containing 0, 1, and 4 shn-1 copies compared to wild type controls
source: Similarly, when compared to wild type controls, gem-4 induction was significantly diminished in animals containing 0, 1, and 4 shn-1 copies (Figure 6E).
evidence: Reporter assay data shown in Figure 6E

claim: L-type calcium current density and gem-4 induction were both sensitive to shn-1 copy number
source: Thus, L-type calcium current density and gem-4 induction were both sensitive to shn-1 copy number.

claim: Increased and decreased shn-1 gene dosage produced similar defects in calcium current and gem-4 induction
source: Interestingly, increased and decreased shn-1 gene dosage produced similar defects in calcium current and gem-4 induction.

claim: Evoked responses were significantly larger in shn-1 null mutants
source: Evoked responses were significantly larger in shn-1 null mutants (Figure 7A,C).

claim: The shape of evoked responses in wild type and shn-1 mutants were indistinguishable
source: The shape of evoked responses in wild type and shn-1 mutants were indistinguishable, indicating that the kinetics of evoked release was unaltered (Figure 7B).

claim: The kinetics of evoked release was unaltered in shn-1 mutants
source: The shape of evoked responses in wild type and shn-1 mutants were indistinguishable, indicating that the kinetics of evoked release was unaltered (Figure 7B).

claim: The rate and amplitude of spontaneous miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) were unaltered in shn-1 mutants
source: The rate and amplitude of spontaneous miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) were unaltered in shn-1 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: The change in evoked EPSC amplitude combined with unaltered mEPSC amplitudes indicates a pre-synaptic change in cholinergic transmission
source: The change in evoked EPSC amplitude combined with unaltered mEPSC amplitudes indicates a pre-synaptic change in cholinergic transmission.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of evoked and miniature EPSCs

claim: The shn-1 null EPSC defect was rescued by transgenes expressing SHN-1 in body muscles
source: The shn-1 null EPSC defect was rescued by transgenes expressing SHN-1 in body muscles, implying that SHN-1 functions post-synaptically (Figure 7B).

claim: SHN-1 functions post-synaptically to regulate evoked EPSCs
source: The shn-1 null EPSC defect was rescued by transgenes expressing SHN-1 in body muscles, implying that SHN-1 functions post-synaptically (Figure 7B).

claim: The evoked EPSCs observed in animals with 1, 2, and 4 shn-1 copies were not significantly different
source: The evoked EPSCs (Figure 7C) and mEPSCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E) observed in animals with 1, 2, and 4 shn-1 copies were not significantly different, indicating that synaptic transmission is not sensitive to shn-1 copy number.

claim: The mEPSCs observed in animals with 1, 2, and 4 shn-1 copies were not significantly different
source: The evoked EPSCs (Figure 7C) and mEPSCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E) observed in animals with 1, 2, and 4 shn-1 copies were not significantly different, indicating that synaptic transmission is not sensitive to shn-1 copy number.
evidence: Electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E

claim: Synaptic transmission is not sensitive to shn-1 copy number
source: The evoked EPSCs (Figure 7C) and mEPSCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E) observed in animals with 1, 2, and 4 shn-1 copies were not significantly different, indicating that synaptic transmission is not sensitive to shn-1 copy number.

claim: Glutamatergic transmission in the striatum was enhanced in Shank3B-/- homozygotes but this effect was not observed in Shank3B+/- heterozygotes
source: Similar results were recently reported in mice where glutamatergic transmission in the striatum was enhanced in Shank3B-/- homozygotes but this effect was not observed in Shank3B+/- heterozygotes (Peixoto et al., 2016).

claim: Shank mutations and copy number variations (CNVs) are linked to several psychiatric disorders
source: Shank mutations and copy number variations (CNVs) are linked to several psychiatric disorders, and to synaptic and behavioral defects in mice.

claim: Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to synaptic and behavioral defects in mice
source: Shank mutations and copy number variations (CNVs) are linked to several psychiatric disorders, and to synaptic and behavioral defects in mice.

claim: Increased and decreased shn-1 gene dosage alter L-channel current
source: Here we show that the C. elegans SHN-1/Shank binds L-type calcium channels and that increased and decreased shn-1 gene dosage alter L-channel current and activity-induced expression of a CRH-1/CREB transcriptional target (gem-4 Copine), which parallels the effects of human Shank copy number variations (CNVs) on Autism spectrum disorders and schizophrenia.

claim: Increased and decreased shn-1 gene dosage alter activity-induced expression of a CRH-1/CREB transcriptional target (gem-4 Copine)
source: Here we show that the C. elegans SHN-1/Shank binds L-type calcium channels and that increased and decreased shn-1 gene dosage alter L-channel current and activity-induced expression of a CRH-1/CREB transcriptional target (gem-4 Copine), which parallels the effects of human Shank copy number variations (CNVs) on Autism spectrum disorders and schizophrenia.

claim: The effects of shn-1 gene dosage on L-channel current and gem-4 expression parallel the effects of human Shank copy number variations (CNVs) on Autism spectrum disorders and schizophrenia
source: Here we show that the C. elegans SHN-1/Shank binds L-type calcium channels and that increased and decreased shn-1 gene dosage alter L-channel current and activity-induced expression of a CRH-1/CREB transcriptional target (gem-4 Copine), which parallels the effects of human Shank copy number variations (CNVs) on Autism spectrum disorders and schizophrenia.
evidence: Comparison between C. elegans and human data

claim: An important function of Shank proteins is to regulate L-channel current and activity induced gene expression
source: These results suggest that an important function of Shank proteins is to regulate L-channel current and activity induced gene expression.

claim: Shank is highly enriched in the post-synaptic densities of excitatory synapses
source: Because Shank is highly enriched in the post-synaptic densities of excitatory synapses, prior studies have focused on the idea that Shank proteins regulate some aspect of synapse formation or function.

claim: Shank proteins bind hundreds of other synaptic proteins through its various domains
source: Through its various domains, Shank proteins bind hundreds of other synaptic proteins (Lee et al., 2011; Sakai et al., 2011) thereby potentially altering diverse cellular functions.

claim: Shank proteins have been implicated in synaptic transmission, synapse formation, synaptic plasticity, and cytoskeletal remodeling
source: Shank proteins have been implicated in synaptic transmission, synapse formation, synaptic plasticity, and cytoskeletal remodeling (Jiang and Ehlers, 2013).

claim: Mammals have three Shank genes, each encoding multiple isoforms
source: Mammals have three Shank genes, each encoding multiple isoforms (Jiang and Ehlers, 2013).

claim: Mouse Shank knockouts exhibit inconsistent (often contradictory) synaptic and behavioral defects
source: Several mouse Shank knockouts have been described but these mutants exhibit inconsistent (often contradictory) synaptic and behavioral defects (Jiang and Ehlers, 2013), most likely resulting from differences in which Shank isoforms are impacted by each mutation.

claim: The inconsistent phenotypes in mouse Shank knockouts most likely result from differences in which Shank isoforms are impacted by each mutation
source: Several mouse Shank knockouts have been described but these mutants exhibit inconsistent (often contradictory) synaptic and behavioral defects (Jiang and Ehlers, 2013), most likely resulting from differences in which Shank isoforms are impacted by each mutation.

claim: The biochemical mechanism by which Shank mutations alter synaptic function and behavior has not been determined
source: The biochemical mechanism by which Shank mutations alter synaptic function and behavior has not been determined.

claim: In humans, Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD), schizophrenia, and mania
source: In humans, Shank mutations and CNVs are linked to Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD), schizophrenia, and mania (Durand et al., 2007; Peça et al., 2011).

claim: Haploinsufficiency for 22q13 (which spans the Shank3 locus) occurs in Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS), a syndromic form of ASD
source: Haploinsufficiency for 22q13 (which spans the Shank3 locus) occurs in Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS), a syndromic form of ASD (Phelan and McDermid, 2012).

claim: PMS patients exhibit autistic behaviors accompanied by hypotonia, delayed speech, and intellectual disability (ID)
source: PMS patients exhibit autistic behaviors accompanied by hypotonia, delayed speech, and intellectual disability (ID) (Bonaglia et al., 2011).

claim: Heterozygous inactivating Shank3 mutations are found in sporadic ASD and schizophrenia
source: Heterozygous inactivating Shank3 mutations are found in sporadic ASD and schizophrenia (Durand et al., 2007; Peça et al., 2011).

claim: Decreased Shank3 function likely plays an important role in the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders
source: These genetic studies suggest that decreased Shank3 function likely plays an important role in the pathophysiology of these psychiatric disorders.

claim: 22q13 duplications spanning Shank3 are found in ASD, schizophrenia, ADHD, and bipolar disorder
source: 22q13 duplications spanning Shank3 are found in ASD, schizophrenia, ADHD, and bipolar disorder (Durand et al., 2007; Failla et al., 2007; Han et al., 2013).

claim: A transgenic mouse model that selectively over-expresses Shank3 exhibited hyperactive behavior and susceptibility to seizures
source: To address this issue, a transgenic mouse model was developed that selectively over-expresses Shank3 (Han et al., 2013). This transgenic mouse exhibited hyperactive behavior and susceptibility to seizures.

claim: Too little or too much Shank3 is associated with several psychiatric disorders
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that too little or too much Shank3 is associated with several psychiatric disorders.

claim: If Shank3 mutations and CNVs are causally associated with psychiatric disorders, cellular and circuit phenotypes should also be sensitive to Shank3 copy number
source: If Shank3 mutations and CNVs are causally associated with these psychiatric disorders, cellular and circuit phenotypes should also be sensitive to Shank3 copy number.

claim: Shank3+/- heterozygotes show decreased mEPSC frequency and spine density
source: Consistent with this idea, several defects have been reported in Shank3+/- heterozygotes, including: decreased mEPSC frequency and spine density (Zhou et al., 2016), decreased Ih current density (Yi et al., 2016), decreased TRPV1 current density (Han et al., 2016), increased tactile sensitivity (Orefice et al., 2016), and decreased post-synaptic Homer abundance (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Shank3+/- heterozygotes show decreased Ih current density
source: Consistent with this idea, several defects have been reported in Shank3+/- heterozygotes, including: decreased mEPSC frequency and spine density (Zhou et al., 2016), decreased Ih current density (Yi et al., 2016), decreased TRPV1 current density (Han et al., 2016), increased tactile sensitivity (Orefice et al., 2016), and decreased post-synaptic Homer abundance (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Shank3+/- heterozygotes show decreased TRPV1 current density
source: Consistent with this idea, several defects have been reported in Shank3+/- heterozygotes, including: decreased mEPSC frequency and spine density (Zhou et al., 2016), decreased Ih current density (Yi et al., 2016), decreased TRPV1 current density (Han et al., 2016), increased tactile sensitivity (Orefice et al., 2016), and decreased post-synaptic Homer abundance (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Shank3+/- heterozygotes show increased tactile sensitivity
source: Consistent with this idea, several defects have been reported in Shank3+/- heterozygotes, including: decreased mEPSC frequency and spine density (Zhou et al., 2016), decreased Ih current density (Yi et al., 2016), decreased TRPV1 current density (Han et al., 2016), increased tactile sensitivity (Orefice et al., 2016), and decreased post-synaptic Homer abundance (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Shank3+/- heterozygotes show decreased post-synaptic Homer abundance
source: Consistent with this idea, several defects have been reported in Shank3+/- heterozygotes, including: decreased mEPSC frequency and spine density (Zhou et al., 2016), decreased Ih current density (Yi et al., 2016), decreased TRPV1 current density (Han et al., 2016), increased tactile sensitivity (Orefice et al., 2016), and decreased post-synaptic Homer abundance (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Increased Shank expression was associated with increased spine density in hippocampus and decreased inhibitory synapses
source: Increased Shank expression was associated with increased spine density in hippocampus and decreased inhibitory synapses (Han et al., 2013).

claim: It remains unclear which Shank binding partners and cellular functions are responsible for psychiatric traits
source: While these studies identify cellular deficits associated with Shank3 CNVs, it remains unclear which Shank binding partners and cellular functions are responsible for psychiatric traits, nor why these traits are sensitive to both increased and decreased Shank gene dosage.

claim: It remains unclear why psychiatric traits are sensitive to both increased and decreased Shank gene dosage
source: While these studies identify cellular deficits associated with Shank3 CNVs, it remains unclear which Shank binding partners and cellular functions are responsible for psychiatric traits, nor why these traits are sensitive to both increased and decreased Shank gene dosage.

claim: C. elegans SHN-1 is a dose-sensitive regulator of Cav1 calcium current in C. elegans body muscles
source: Here we show that C. elegans SHN-1 is a dose-sensitive regulator of Cav1 calcium current and CREB induced gene expression in C. elegans body muscles.

claim: C. elegans SHN-1 is a dose-sensitive regulator of CREB induced gene expression in C. elegans body muscles
source: Here we show that C. elegans SHN-1 is a dose-sensitive regulator of Cav1 calcium current and CREB induced gene expression in C. elegans body muscles.

claim: Human CACNA1C (which encodes a Cav1 α-subunit) is mutated in Timothy Syndrome (TS), a rare monogenic form of ASD
source: Of these potential binding partners, we focused on EGL-19/Cav1 because human CACNA1C (which encodes a Cav1 α-subunit) is mutated in Timothy Syndrome (TS), a rare monogenic form of ASD (Splawski et al., 2005, 2004), and polymorphisms linked to CACNA1C are associated with multiple psychiatric disorders (Cross-Disorder Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2013).

claim: Polymorphisms linked to CACNA1C are associated with multiple psychiatric disorders
source: Of these potential binding partners, we focused on EGL-19/Cav1 because human CACNA1C (which encodes a Cav1 α-subunit) is mutated in Timothy Syndrome (TS), a rare monogenic form of ASD (Splawski et al., 2005, 2004), and polymorphisms linked to CACNA1C are associated with multiple psychiatric disorders (Cross-Disorder Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2013).

claim: The carboxy-terminus of mammalian Cav1.3 (-ITTLCOOH) is predicted to bind PDZ domains
source: The carboxy-terminus of mammalian Cav1.3 (-ITTLCOOH) and Cav1.2 (-VSSLCOOH) channels are both predicted to bind PDZ domains (Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: The carboxy-terminus of mammalian Cav1.2 (-VSSLCOOH) is predicted to bind PDZ domains
source: The carboxy-terminus of mammalian Cav1.3 (-ITTLCOOH) and Cav1.2 (-VSSLCOOH) channels are both predicted to bind PDZ domains (Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: When mutant constructs lacking the carboxy-terminal PDZ ligands of Cav1.3 or Cav1.2 channels were expressed in hippocampal neurons, no changes in calcium current were observed
source: When mutant constructs lacking the carboxy-terminal PDZ ligands of Cav1.3 or Cav1.2 channels were expressed in hippocampal neurons, no changes in calcium current were observed; however, the Cav1.3 truncation mutant exhibited decreased synaptic localization (Weick et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: The Cav1.3 truncation mutant lacking the carboxy-terminal PDZ ligand exhibited decreased synaptic localization
source: When mutant constructs lacking the carboxy-terminal PDZ ligands of Cav1.3 or Cav1.2 channels were expressed in hippocampal neurons, no changes in calcium current were observed; however, the Cav1.3 truncation mutant exhibited decreased synaptic localization (Weick et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: The rat Shank 1 and 3 PDZ domains exhibit strong binding to Cav1.3 (but not Cav1.2)
source: The rat Shank 1 and 3 PDZ domains exhibit strong binding to Cav1.3 (but not Cav1.2).

claim: Shank proteins could promote synaptic targeting of Cav1.3
source: Thus, Shank proteins could promote synaptic targeting of Cav1.3; however, the PDZ protein responsible for Cav1.3 targeting has not been identified.

claim: The PDZ protein responsible for Cav1.3 targeting has not been identified
source: Thus, Shank proteins could promote synaptic targeting of Cav1.3; however, the PDZ protein responsible for Cav1.3 targeting has not been identified.

claim: Deleting the carboxy-terminal PDZ ligand in Cav1.2 or 1.3 diminishes activity-induced CREB phosphorylation and transcription of CREB targets
source: These studies showed that deleting the carboxy-terminal PDZ ligand in Cav1.2 or 1.3, or over-expressing peptides containing the PDZ-ligands diminish activity-induced CREB phosphorylation and transcription of CREB targets.

claim: Over-expressing peptides containing the PDZ-ligands of Cav1.2 or 1.3 diminishes activity-induced CREB phosphorylation and transcription of CREB targets
source: These studies showed that deleting the carboxy-terminal PDZ ligand in Cav1.2 or 1.3, or over-expressing peptides containing the PDZ-ligands diminish activity-induced CREB phosphorylation and transcription of CREB targets.

claim: Calcium current density and induced gem-4 expression were poorly correlated
source: A puzzling aspect of our results is that calcium current density and induced gem-4 expression were poorly correlated.

claim: CREB phosphorylation was poorly correlated with calcium current density in cultured mammalian neurons
source: Similar results were also reported in cultured mammalian neurons, where CREB phosphorylation was poorly correlated with calcium current density and instead was better correlated with Cav1 open probability (Wheeler et al., 2008).

claim: CREB phosphorylation was better correlated with Cav1 open probability than with calcium current density in cultured mammalian neurons
source: Similar results were also reported in cultured mammalian neurons, where CREB phosphorylation was poorly correlated with calcium current density and instead was better correlated with Cav1 open probability (Wheeler et al., 2008).

claim: CREB phosphorylation is mediated by a calcium sensor that is spatially very close to (and possibly physically associated with) activated Cav1 channels
source: Based on these results (and others), these authors proposed that CREB phosphorylation is mediated by a calcium sensor that is spatially very close to (and possibly physically associated with) activated Cav1 channels (Deisseroth et al., 1996; Wheeler et al., 2008).

claim: CREB phosphorylation would be strongly correlated with calcium levels in the nanodomain of a Cav1 channel but less correlated with global cytoplasmic calcium
source: In this scenario, CREB phosphorylation would be strongly correlated with calcium levels in the nanodomain of a Cav1 channel but less correlated with global cytoplasmic calcium.

claim: CRH-1 activation may be mediated by tight coupling of a calcium sensor to activated EGL-19/Cav1 channels
source: Thus, our results suggest that CRH-1 activation may also be mediated by tight coupling of a calcium sensor to activated EGL-19/Cav1 channels.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and literature

claim: In humans, Shank deletions and duplications both confer risk for ASD and schizophrenia
source: In humans, Shank deletions and duplications both confer risk for ASD and schizophrenia (Bonaglia et al., 2006; Durand et al., 2007; Failla et al., 2007; Gauthier et al., 2010; Han et al., 2013).

claim: If Shank CNVs are causally linked to psychiatric disorders, cellular defects linked to ASD should exhibit similar sensitivity to Shank gene dosage
source: If Shank CNVs are causally linked to these psychiatric disorders, cellular defects linked to ASD should exhibit similar sensitivity to Shank gene dosage.

claim: Changes in shn-1 gene dosage alter two cell autonomous phenotypes in muscles: L-channel calcium current and expression of CREB target genes
source: Here we find that changes in shn-1 gene dosage alter two cell autonomous phenotypes in muscles: L-channel calcium current and expression of CREB target genes.

claim: Similar defects in L-channel calcium current and CREB target expression were observed in muscles with decreased and increased shn-1 dosage
source: For both phenotypes, similar defects were observed in muscles with decreased and increased shn-1 dosage.

claim: Human Shank CNVs also cause cellular phenotypes, which may include altered calcium current and CREB target expression
source: Based on these results, we propose that human Shank CNVs also cause cellular phenotypes, which may include altered calcium current and CREB target expression.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation from C. elegans to human

claim: Sensitivity to Shank copy number provides a useful criterion to determine which phenotypes are more likely to contribute to the psychiatric traits associated with Shank CNVs
source: Thus, sensitivity to Shank copy number provides a useful criterion to determine which phenotypes are more likely to contribute to the psychiatric traits associated with Shank CNVs.

claim: Shank3 binds directly to Ih and TRPV1 channels in neurons
source: Two recent studies showed that Shank3 binds directly to Ih and TRPV1 channels in neurons and that the corresponding currents densities are significantly reduced in Shank3+/- heterozygotes (Han et al., 2016; Yi et al., 2016).

claim: Ih and TRPV1 current densities are significantly reduced in Shank3+/- heterozygotes
source: Two recent studies showed that Shank3 binds directly to Ih and TRPV1 channels in neurons and that the corresponding currents densities are significantly reduced in Shank3+/- heterozygotes (Han et al., 2016; Yi et al., 2016).

claim: An important function of Shank proteins is to regulate ion channel densities
source: These results (together with those reported here) suggest that an important function of Shank proteins is to regulate ion channel densities.

claim: Dosage sensitive phenotypes are thought to occur by disrupting the function of multimeric protein complexes
source: In general, dosage sensitive phenotypes are thought to occur by disrupting the function of multimeric protein complexes.

claim: Under and over-expression of individual subunits alter the stoichiometry of assembled holo-complexes, leading to decreased activity
source: In such cases, under and over-expression of individual subunits alter the stoichiometry of assembled holo-complexes, leading to decreased activity.

claim: Increased and decreased expression of the yeast histones H2A and H2B results in similar loss of function phenotypes (chromosome loss and altered gene expression)
source: For example, increased and decreased expression of the yeast histones H2A and H2B results in similar loss of function phenotypes (chromosome loss and altered gene expression) (Clark-Adams et al., 1988; Meeks-Wagner and Hartwell, 1986).

claim: Shank undergoes zinc induced polymerization into large complexes
source: Shank binds many other synaptic proteins (Lee et al., 2011; Sakai et al., 2011) and undergoes zinc induced polymerization into large complexes (Baron et al., 2006; Hayashi et al., 2009).

claim: Increased and decreased Shank abundance could disrupt the stoichiometry of post-synaptic complexes
source: Thus, increased and decreased Shank abundance could disrupt the stoichiometry of post-synaptic complexes.
evidence: Inferred from Shank's properties and general principles

claim: L-current and CREB activation are sensitive to subtle changes in the stoichiometry of Shank protein complexes
source: Our results suggest that L-current and CREB activation are sensitive to subtle changes in the stoichiometry of Shank protein complexes.

claim: Dynamic changes in the composition of Shank complexes provides a mechanism to regulate circuit function and plasticity (and potentially psychiatric traits)
source: Our results further suggest that dynamic changes in the composition of Shank complexes provides a mechanism to regulate circuit function and plasticity (and potentially psychiatric traits).

claim: Shank regulation of L-currents and CREB activation could both contribute to the pathophysiology of ASD
source: Shank regulation of L-currents and CREB activation could both contribute to the pathophysiology of ASD.

claim: Human Shank mutations are particularly linked to ASD associated with intellectual disability
source: Human Shank mutations are particularly linked to ASD associated with intellectual disability (Leblond et al., 2014).

claim: CREB has long been linked to learning and memory in several model organisms
source: CREB has long been linked to learning and memory in several model organisms (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Dash et al., 1990; Yin et al., 1994); consequently, Shank's CREB activation function could directly contribute to cognitive deficits associated humans Shank CNVs.

claim: Shank's CREB activation function could directly contribute to cognitive deficits associated with human Shank CNVs
source: CREB has long been linked to learning and memory in several model organisms (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Dash et al., 1990; Yin et al., 1994); consequently, Shank's CREB activation function could directly contribute to cognitive deficits associated humans Shank CNVs.

claim: CREB-induced BDNF expression promotes development of inhibitory synapses in the cortex
source: CREB-induced BDNF expression promotes development of inhibitory synapses in the cortex (Hong et al., 2008).

claim: Shank's CREB activation function could alter synaptic inhibition, a phenotype found in several ASD models
source: Thus, Shank's CREB activation function could alter synaptic inhibition, a phenotype found in several ASD models (Dani et al., 2005; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003).

claim: L-channels play an important role in calcium signaling in dendrites and spines
source: Finally, L-channels play an important role in calcium signaling in dendrites and spines (Higley and Sabatini, 2012).

claim: Shank's Cav1 current density function could contribute to cognitive or developmental defects in ASD by adjusting dendritic calcium signaling in CNS neurons
source: Thus, Shank's Cav1 current density function could contribute to cognitive or developmental defects in ASD by adjusting dendritic calcium signaling in CNS neurons.

claim: Shank effects on Cav1 currents and CREB target expression could play an important role in the pathophysiology of ASD (and potentially other psychiatric disorders)
source: For these reasons, we propose that Shank effects on Cav1 currents and CREB target expression could play an important role in the pathophysiology of ASD (and potentially other psychiatric disorders).
evidence: Speculative proposal based on experimental findings

claim: shn-1 is expressed in muscles
source: Because shn-1 is expressed in muscles (Stefanakis et al., 2015), we assayed EGL-19/Cav1 channel function by recording voltage-activated calcium currents in body muscle, using salines containing potassium channel blockers (TEA and 4AP).

claim: In the recording conditions used, the remaining voltage-activated inward current is entirely blocked by the EGL-19 antagonist nemadipine
source: In these conditions, the remaining voltage-activated inward current is entirely blocked by the EGL-19 antagonist nemadipine (Lainé et al., 2011).

claim: The magnitude of gating currents can be used as a measure of Cav channel surface abundance
source: The magnitude of gating currents can be used as a measure of Cav channel surface abundance (Fu et al., 2011; Hulme et al., 2006).

claim: The shn-1 mutant defect in gating charge is unlikely to result from decreased surface delivery of other voltage-activated channels because voltage-activated potassium currents were unaltered in shn-1 mutants
source: This shn-1 mutant defect in gating charge is unlikely to result from decreased surface delivery of other voltage-activated channels because voltage-activated potassium currents were unaltered in shn-1 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from selective effect on gating charge but not K+ currents

claim: In patch clamp recordings of body muscles, spontaneous action potentials are observed at ~1 Hz
source: In patch clamp recordings of body muscles, spontaneous action potentials are observed at ~1 Hz (Gao and Zhen, 2011).

claim: unc-13 mutants have dramatically reduced synaptic vesicle exocytosis
source: Photo-induction of gem-4 expression was eliminated in unc-13 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which have dramatically reduced synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Richmond et al., 1999).
